name: Reciprocity

pinned_evidence.title: The Norm of Reciprocity: A Preliminary Statement
Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique
pinned_evidence.reason: reciprocity in compliance — Cialdini et al.

evidence.basis: The reciprocity norm — a felt obligation to return benefits received — is a broadly documented social rule (Gouldner 1960) and underlies compliance techniques like door-in-the-face (Cialdini). Field experiments (gift-exchange) show reciprocal behavior reliably.
evidence.effect_size_note: Reciprocity effects are real and cross-culturally present, but the magnitude in commercial contexts depends on the gift feeling genuine and unconditional; transparent quid-pro-quo weakens it.

mechanism_summary_for_context: Receiving something creates a felt obligation to give back. Deliver genuine value first — a useful free tool, real help, an unexpected upgrade — and users are more inclined to reciprocate with attention, signup, or purchase. The value given must be genuine and useful on its own; reciprocity engineered as a transparent transaction ('we gave you X so now you owe us') backfires. Ventora's lead-magnet funnels are reciprocity in action.

preconditions.reason: requires real value delivered before the ask; not applicable where nothing genuine is given first

applicability.culture_note: Reciprocity is a near-universal social norm; its strength and the acceptable form of gifts vary culturally; an L3 surface parameter

implementations.generation_directive: Deliver genuine, useful value before asking for anything — a real free result, tool, or insight the user keeps regardless. The gift must stand on its own as useful; the ask follows naturally, not as an explicit price for the gift. Ventora's free Idea Check report is the pattern.

Give an unexpected, genuine benefit (a surprise upgrade, extra credits, a bonus) without demanding return. Unconditional giving reciprocates more strongly than conditional. Never frame it as a debt to be repaid.

hard_rules.rule: The value given must be genuinely useful on its own; hollow 'gifts' engineered solely to create obligation are forbidden
Do not frame the gift as a debt or pressure repayment; reciprocity must remain a free response, not a manufactured obligation
Do not use unsolicited 'gifts' (e.g. forced trials that auto-bill) as reciprocity leverage

constraints.boundary_test: Is the value given genuinely useful and freely given — or a hollow gift engineered to manufacture obligation?

relations.note: A received gift can become 'owned' (endowment); distinct — reciprocity is obligation-to-return, endowment is valuation-of-owned
Both are social-norm mechanisms but differ: reciprocity is exchange obligation, social proof is others-as-evidence

reference_examples.product: Free tools / lead magnets (HubSpot, Ventora Idea Check)
reference_examples.what: Genuine free value delivered first creates reciprocity toward signup/purchase — the canonical value-first pattern
Free sample creates mild reciprocal obligation to consider buying — classic in-person reciprocity
Unexpected unconditional benefit reciprocates as loyalty and goodwill
